claims.text: Multi-principal-element mixing enhances lattice distortion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases the energy barriers to dislocation motion.
Enhanced lattice distortion alters phonon-scattering behavior.
The effects of lattice distortion on dislocations and phonons improve high-temperature yield strength.
The effects of lattice distortion on dislocations and phonons reduce high-temperature creep.
The effects of lattice distortion on dislocations and phonons promote reversible thermoelastic behavior.
The alloys considered can be prepared as single-phase, fully crystallized materials with homogeneous elemental distributions and minimal secondary-phase precipitates.
Changing elemental ratios can systematically vary lattice distortion.
Enhanced lattice distortion is associated with sluggish diffusion.
Increased lattice strain and modified phonon scattering stabilize the microstructure against creep.
Modified phonon-scattering dynamics enable reversible thermoelastic responses during high-temperature thermal cycling.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, alloys with greater lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than lower-distortion baselines.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, alloys with greater lattice distortion will have lower creep rates than lower-distortion baselines.
Under identical high-temperature conditions, alloys with greater lattice distortion will exhibit more robust thermoelastic recovery than lower-distortion baselines.
At temperatures of approximately 800 degrees Celsius or higher, diffusion and dislocation mechanisms are critical to the behavior under study.
The influence of lattice distortion may be diminished at lower temperatures.
